value.narrative_en: Recognition of Forest Sámi (metsälappalaiset) as an indigenous Sámi group
value.historical_note_en: In linguistics, Kemi Sámi is classified as an extinct Sámi language that died out in the 19th century with only limited fragmentary records surviving, and the status of modern 'Forest Sámi' as a Sámi group is contested in Finland and not recognised by the Sámi Parliament.

Another editor reverted the overhaul for reducing a substantial article into a stub.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted multiple repetitive passages arguing on the basis of a single Suomen Kuvalehti magazine article that Sámi identity is less than a century old, that the Sámi are no more indigenous than Finns, and that talk of colonialism or forced displacement is false. Through a wholesale revert to an older revision, the edit also stripped images, citations to the Sámi Parliament, and recent maintenance edits, while adding citation-quality tags questioning Sámi sources.
evidence: Saamelaiset eivät ole alkuperäisempiä kuin suomalaiset, vaikka heitä kutsutaan [[alkuperäiskansa]]ksi.
value.claim_en: Sámi identity and languages are relatively recent developments, the Sámi are no more indigenous to Finland than Finns, and their assimilation was voluntary rather than the result of colonialism or forced displacement.
value.claim_fi: Saamelainen identiteetti ja saamen kielet ovat suhteellisen nuoria, saamelaiset eivät ole Suomessa suomalaisia alkuperäisempiä, ja heidän sulautumisensa suomalaisiin oli vapaaehtoista eikä kolonialismin tai pakottamisen seurausta.
value.narrative_en: Challenging Sámi indigenous status and colonial history in Finland
value.historical_note_en: In historical linguistics, the divergence of Proto-Samic and Proto-Finnic is dated to around 2,500–3,000 years ago rather than less than a thousand years ago as the edit claims.
value.uncertainty_note: The diff appears to aggregate or restore an older revision during an edit war (hence the duplicated paragraphs in inserted_text and loss of unrelated images/maintenance), so some removed items are collateral damage from a clumsy revert rather than individually targeted deletions.

value.what_changed_en: The edit added several unsourced sentences about Finnish kings in neighboring legends, the 1187 destruction of Sigtuna, Johannes Messenius's writings, and royal titles used by Swedish and Russian monarchs, while also softening the sourced statement that 'kuningas' derives from Proto-Germanic into merely having a Proto-Germanic counterpart. It was reverted as unsourced additions.
evidence: Suomen kuninkaiden historiaa kuvaa laajimmin 1600-luvulla ruotsalainen historioitsija [[Johannes Messenius]], teoksessaan [[Scondia illustrata|Scondia illustrata.]]

Historiallisena aikana kukaan Ruotsin kuninkaista tai Venäjän tsaareista ei ole käyttänyt titteleissään nimitystä 'Suomen Kuningas', kiistanalaista [[Kaarle IX]]:ttä (hallitsijana 1604-1611) lukuunottamatta.
value.claim_en: The word 'kuningas' merely has a counterpart in Proto-Germanic rather than deriving from it, and Finnish kings are widely remembered as adversaries in neighboring traditions and described in detail by Johannes Messenius, while later Swedish and Russian rulers (except arguably Charles IX) did not use the title 'King of Finland'.
value.claim_fi: Sanalla 'kuningas' on vain vastine muinaisgermaanissa lainautumisen sijaan, suomalaisten kuninkaat muistetaan laajalti vastustajina naapurikansojen tarinoissa sekä Johannes Messeniuksen teoksessa, eivätkä myöhemmät Ruotsin tai Venäjän hallitsijat kiistanalaista Kaarle IX:ää lukuun ottamatta käyttäneet titteliä 'Suomen kuningas'.
value.narrative_en: Romanticised or pseudohistorical emphasis on ancient Finnish kingship
value.historical_note_en: In historical linguistics it is well established that Finnic 'kuningas' is a loanword borrowed from Proto-Germanic '*kuningaz', not merely an independent word with a Germanic counterpart, and the title 'Grand Duke' dates to the 1580s under John III rather than 1556 (when he became Duke of Finland).
value.uncertainty_note: The edit mixes plausible historical trivia, minor factual inaccuracies, unsourced synthesis, and subtle framing shifts (such as downplaying Germanic loanword origin on a frequent pseudohistory topic in Finland), making it borderline between pov_push, good_faith_error, and source_manipulation.

value.what_changed_en: Added a paragraph arguing that Tacitus's description of the Fenni was an accurate but narrow account derived from foreign fur traders visiting temporary coastal marketplaces, citing unrelated works and other Wikipedia articles as sources. The reverter removed it as off-topic speculation, original research, and invalid self-sourcing.
evidence: Toisaalta kuvaus vastaa hyvin suomalaisen eräperinteen ja naisten tasa-arvon tutkimusta.
Näin ollen ulkomaalaiset turkiskauppiaat näkivät vain markkinapaikan tilapäisiä asumuksia kuten havulaavuja tms. ja tapasivat lähinnä turkiksia kauppaamassa olleita metsästäjäperheitä
Nyt artikkeliin on lisätty spekulaatiota, jopa omaa tutkimusta, joka menee asiasta sivuun. Eikä wikipediakaan kelpaa itsensä lähteeksi.
value.claim_en: Tacitus's description of the Fenni aligns with Finnish wilderness tradition and gender equality research, representing a narrow but accurate view formed by foreign fur traders visiting temporary seasonal trading posts.
value.claim_fi: Tacituksen kuvaus fenneistä vastaa suomalaisen eräperinteen ja naisten tasa-arvon tutkimusta ja on kapea mutta oikea kuvaus, joka syntyi ulkomaisten turkiskauppiaiden vieraillessa tilapäisillä markkinapaikoilla.
value.narrative_en: Equating ancient Fenni directly with historical Finns and romanticising early Finnish society
value.historical_note_en: It is not established who the Fenni mentioned by Tacitus were—many scholars associate them more closely with ancestors of the Sámi or generic northern hunter-gatherers rather than Iron Age agriculturalist ancestors of Finns—and Tacitus's account relies heavily on classical ethnographic tropes about 'noble savages' rather than eyewitness reports from Viking-Age-style coastal trading posts.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit combines original research (synthesising unrelated sources like a wilderness skills manual, a Viking Age urbanization study, and Wikipedia articles) with a subtle nationalist/romanticised framing equating the Fenni with Finnish heritage, making 'pov_push' or 'source_manipulation' plausible secondary categories, though the editor's tone appears sincere.

value.what_changed_en: Across a sequence of edits over three months, editors removed a sourced passage arguing from a Suomen Kuvalehti article that Finns and Sámi are equally indigenous and differentiated only in recent centuries, while adding images, demographic figures, and details on Sámi languages spoken in Finland. The reverter restored the removed sourced text.

Suomessa puhutaan kolmea saamen kieltä: pohjois-, inarin ja koltansaamea, jotka ovat kaikki uhanalaisia.
value.claim_en: Three endangered Sámi languages—Northern, Inari, and Skolt Sámi—are spoken in Finland, and 75% of Sámi children under 10 live outside the Sámi homeland, while claims that Finns and Sámi are equally indigenous and recently differentiated should be omitted.
value.claim_fi: Suomessa puhutaan kolmea uhanalaista saamen kieltä (pohjois-, inarin- ja koltansaamea) ja 75 % alle 10-vuotiaista saamelaisista asuu saamelaisalueen ulkopuolella, kun taas väitteet suomalaisten ja saamelaisten yhtäläisestä alkuperäisyydestä ja myöhäisestä eriytymisestä tulisi jättää pois.
value.narrative_en: Debate over Sámi indigeneity and historical origins in Finland
value.uncertainty_note: The diff aggregates three months of edits by multiple editors (including image restorations, copyedits, and sourced additions alongside the removal of a controversial Suomen Kuvalehti passage), making it unclear whether the revert targeted only the unexplained removal of sourced text (source_manipulation / pov_push) or was a broader content_dispute.

value.what_changed_en: Added a sourced clause qualifying a statement about the Sámi's status by noting that there are other state-recognized and self-declared indigenous peoples in Europe (such as Livonians, Karelians, and Võros), and re-inserted a sourced sentence stating that the Constitution of Finland recognizes the Sámi's indigenous status and cultural autonomy.
evidence: mutta Euroopassa on myös muita alkuperäiskansoja, osa valtiotasolla sellaisiksi tunnustettuja, osa itse sellaisiksi julistautuneita.
Saamelaisten asema alkuperäiskansana ja kulttuuri-itsehallinto on tunnustettu [[Suomen perustuslaki|Suomen perustuslaissa]].
nyt lukija voi saada sellaisen käsityksen, että saamelaiset olisivat EU:n alueen ainoa alkup.kansa, jolla on jokin tunnustettu asema.
Kansalliset kielipolitiikat muilla alueilla eivät liity aiheeseen.
value.claim_en: There are other state-recognized and self-declared indigenous peoples in Europe besides the Sámi, and the Sámi's status as an indigenous people with cultural autonomy is recognized in the Constitution of Finland.
value.claim_fi: Euroopassa on saamelaisten lisäksi myös muita valtiotasolla tunnustettuja tai itse julistautuneita alkuperäiskansoja, ja saamelaisten asema alkuperäiskansana sekä kulttuuri-itsehallinto on tunnustettu Suomen perustuslaissa.
value.narrative_en: Contextualizing or relativizing the uniqueness of Sámi indigenous status in Europe
value.uncertainty_note: The edit relies on synthesizing examples of individual peoples (Livonians, Karelians, Võros) to qualify the standard EU-level claim that the Sámi are the EU's only recognized indigenous people; this borders on original research or mild POV pushing, though the exchange of edit summaries reflects an editorial disagreement over scope, relevance, and clarity.

The community reverted it as original research and irrelevant.

value.claim_en: The existence of 'Kuningas' as a personal name in medieval Finland does not preclude the existence of actual kings, just as 'King' exists as a surname in England despite England having had Iron Age monarchs.
value.claim_fi: Kuningas-nimen esiintyminen henkilönimenä keskiajan Suomessa ei sulje pois todellisten kuninkaiden olemassaoloa, aivan kuten Englannissa King on sukunimi rautakautisista kuninkaista huolimatta.
value.narrative_en: Promoting the existence of ancient Finnish kings
value.uncertainty_note: The edit borders on 'content_dispute' or 'good_faith_error' (unsourced original research / synthesis), as the literal facts stated about English surnames are true, though synthesized to push a fringe historical viewpoint ('Suomen muinaiset kuninkaat' is a classic Finnish pseudohistory/national-romantic topic).

value.what_changed_en: Rewrote the lead and sections on the origin of Finns to remove the statement that their genetic foundation formed in the Volga–Oka–Kama region of Russia, replacing it with claims—backed by older newspaper articles—that Finns' genetic roots are mainly in Central Europe, that Finno-Ugric speakers were merely 'immigrants' who left only a small genetic trace, and adding a section on 'Ancient Germans' preceding them.
evidence: Tällä alueella syntyi myös tulevien itämerensuomalaisten [[Perinnöllisyystiede|geneettinen]] perusta.
Suomalais-ugrilaista kieltä puhuneet maahanmuuttajat saapuivat nykyisen [[Venäjä|Venäjän]] alueella sijaitsevien [[Volga]]-, [[Oka]]- ja [[Kama]]-jokien alueelta
Emme siis ole mitenkään erityisesti juuri Volgan mutkasta saapuneiden maahanmuuttajien jälkeläisiä, vaan suurin osa Suomeen tulleista esi-isistämme oli peräisin Keski-Euroopasta.
value.claim_en: Modern Finns derive most of their genetic ancestry from Central Europe and earlier Germanic inhabitants rather than from Finno-Ugric-speaking migrants from the Volga–Oka–Kama region.
value.claim_fi: Nykysuomalaisten geneettiset juuret ovat pääosin Keski-Euroopassa ja aiemmissa muinaisgermaanisissa asukkaissa eivätkä Volgan–Okan–Kaman alueelta saapuneissa suomalais-ugrilaista kieltä puhuneissa muuttajissa.
value.narrative_en: Emphasising Western/Central European genetic origins of Finns over eastern Uralic roots
value.uncertainty_note: Borders on content_dispute because both Central European autosomal ancestry and Siberian/Volga-Uralic Y-chromosomal/autosomal components exist in Finnish genetics, and the reverter objected partly on scope ('Artikkeli käsittelee suomalaisten alkuperää' vs. all prehistoric inhabitants of Finland); however, replacing recent scholarly synthesis (Lang 2020) with older news articles (2008, 2015) and repeatedly framing Finno-Ugric speakers as 'immigrants' leaving 'only a small genetic memory' pushes a clear narrative.

The reverter removed the additions for diverging from the first source, lacking page numbers and proper formatting, citing an off-topic dissertation, and placing unsourced material solely in the lead.

Teksti poikkeaa ensimmäisessä virkkeessä liikaa lähteestä. Toisesta ei selviä, mistä kohtaa viitatuista lähteistä tämä väite on.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted a long section claiming that conquerors and biased scholars have censored Finland's true history—alleging even a death penalty under Swedish rule for recounting it—and presenting mythological saga figures as a chronological list of real ancient kings of Finland. The reverter removed it with the summary 'huuhaat pois' ('out with the pseudoscience/nonsense').
evidence: Suomen historiaa on vääristelty ja yritetty tuhota valloittajien toimesta satoja vuosia
Ruotsin vallan aikan oli säädetty jopa kuolemantuomio sille joka kertoisi suomen historiasta.
value.claim_en: Finland had a pre-Swedish dynasty of ancient kings documented in Norse sagas and early chronicles, knowledge of which was deliberately suppressed and censored by foreign conquerors and biased historians.
value.claim_fi: Suomella oli ennen Ruotsin valtaa saagoissa ja vanhoissa kronikoissa dokumentoitu muinaisten kuninkaiden dynastia, jota koskevaa tietoa vieraat valloittajat ja puolueelliset tutkijat ovat tarkoituksellisesti sensuroineet ja vääristelleet.
value.narrative_en: Finnish pseudohistorical 'ancient kings' conspiracy theory
value.historical_note_en: Mainstream historical and archaeological scholarship finds no evidence of a unified prehistoric Finnish kingdom, regards saga figures like Fornjótr as mythological rather than historical monarchs, and knows of no Swedish law punishing the telling of Finnish history with death.
value.uncertainty_note: Overlaps strongly with false_factual_claim (e.g. the fabricated death-penalty law under Swedish rule and treating mythological beings/LDS genealogical entries as dated monarchs), while the overarching conspiracy framing makes pov_push the primary fit.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted an unsourced paragraph of original research claiming that Western Finns are genetically Franks who lived in Southwest Finland before Finns, arguing that the Aura River is named after Franconian 'Aurach' rivers.
evidence: Kun siis kun frankit asuivat Varsinais-Suomessa ennen suomalaisia he aivan varmasti kutsuivat pikkujokeamme nimellä Aurach.
Olemme siis frankkeja, jotka olemme omaksuneet myöhempien tulokkaiden suomenkielen.
value.claim_en: Western Finns are of Frankish descent, Franks inhabited Southwest Finland prior to Finns and named the Aura River after Franconian 'Aurach' rivers before adopting the Finnish language.
value.claim_fi: Länsisuomalaiset ovat perimältään frankkeja, jotka asuivat Varsinais-Suomessa ennen suomalaisia, antoivat Aurajoelle nimen frankkilaisten Aurach-jokien mukaan ja omaksuivat myöhemmin suomen kielen.
value.narrative_en: Pseudohistorical Germanic/Frankish origin theory of Finns
value.historical_note_en: There is no historical, archaeological, or linguistic evidence of a Frankish population inhabiting Southwest Finland, and the name of the Aura River derives from an archaic Scandinavian or Finnish word related to water or plowing rather than Franconian 'Aurach'.
value.uncertainty_note: The edit combines pseudohistorical claims, original research, and an unencyclopedic first-person tone ('Olemme siis frankkeja!'); it could also be viewed as a good_faith_error (sincere amateur folk etymology) or pov_push, or potentially elaborate satire.

value.what_changed_en: Changed the article from past tense to present tense to present the Kemi Sámi (equated with 'Forest Sámi') as an existing people rather than a historically assimilated group, added an unsourced population estimate of 5,000–15,000, and softened statements about the loss of their culture and Sámi identity. The reverter rejected the edit as unsourced original research.
value.claim_en: The Kemi Sámi (Forest Sámi) still exist today as a distinct people numbering approximately 5,000 to 15,000, with much of their culture preserved.
value.claim_fi: Keminsaamelaiset eli metsäsaamelaiset ovat yhä olemassa oleva kansa, johon kuuluu arviolta 5 000–15 000 henkeä ja jonka kulttuuri on säilynyt.
value.narrative_en: Modern Forest Sámi / Kemi Sámi identity and continuity movement in Finland
value.historical_note_en: In mainstream ethnography and linguistics, the Kemi Sámi language became extinct in the 19th century and the historical Kemi Sámi population assimilated into neighbouring Finnish and Sámi populations.
value.uncertainty_note: Overlaps closely with false_factual_claim due to the unsourced 5,000–15,000 population figure, though the overarching motivation is advancing a contested contemporary Indigenous identity narrative.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted claims and a Helsingin Sanomat citation stating that based on ancient DNA, the ancestors of the Sámi likely formed the original population of Finland, and that linguists suggest Sámi languages were spoken there (especially in South Ostrobothnia until the late 11th century) before early Finns arrived. The edit also introduced grammatical breakage, removed hedged phrasing ('though not certain'), and duplicated a sentence, prompting a revert noting that the issue is much more complex and requires deeper discussion.
evidence: Muinais-dna:han perustuvan tutkimustiedon mukaan saamelaisten esivanhemmat muodostivat todennäköisesti Suomen alkuperäisen väestön
Varsinkin Etelä-Pohjanmaalla on arveltu puhutun eteläistä saamen murretta aina 1000-luvun lopulle, jolloin suomen varhaiset muodot syrjäyttivät sen.
Kysymys on huomattavasti monimutkaisempi ja vaatii syvemmän keskustelun.
value.claim_en: Ancient DNA indicates that the ancestors of the Sámi probably formed the original population of Finland, and Sámi languages were spoken across the region before the arrival of the ancestors of modern Finns.
value.claim_fi: Muinais-DNA:n perusteella saamelaisten esivanhemmat muodostivat todennäköisesti Suomen alkuperäisen väestön, ja alueella puhuttiin saamen kieliä ennen nykysuomalaisten esivanhempien saapumista.
value.narrative_en: Sámi primacy as the original indigenous population of Finland
value.historical_note_en: While Iron Age ancient DNA from Levänluhta (South Ostrobothnia) shows genetic affinity to modern Sámi, the earliest Mesolithic post-glacial inhabitants of Finland belonged to distinct hunter-gatherer populations prior to the Bronze/Iron Age arrival of Uralic languages and Siberian-related ancestry.
value.uncertainty_note: Without seeing the exact surrounding sentences beyond the truncated context, it is difficult to tell how much of the awkward syntax and duplication was accidental editing error (good_faith_error) versus deliberate overstatement of a newspaper source (content_dispute or pov_push).

value.claim_fi: Metsäsaamelaiset ovat yksi Suomen saamelaisryhmistä, ja jotkut saamelaiset puhuvat edelleen keminsaamea, jota pidetään virheellisesti kuolleena kielenä.

value.historical_note_en: In linguistics, Kemi Sámi is established as an extinct language whose last native speakers died in the 19th century, and self-identified Forest Sámi (metsälappalaiset) are not officially recognised as a Sámi group by the Sámi Parliament of Finland.
value.uncertainty_note: Combines a strong POV push regarding the contested indigenous identity of Forest Sámi with a false factual claim about Kemi Sámi still being spoken, while also altering sourced sentences without changing the citations.

value.historical_note_en: The Kalevala is a 19th-century literary epic compiled and partly composed by Elias Lönnrot from oral folk poetry, whereas pre-Christian Finnish folk beliefs were diverse local traditions rather than a unified 'Kalevala religion' (a modern term associated with neopaganism, such as Karhun kansa / karuse.info).
value.uncertainty_note: The edit also involves source manipulation (attributing claims about 'Kalevala faith' to mainstream scholars Vahtola and Kuusi while linking a neopagan site) and false factual conflation of the 19th-century epic with medieval folk religion, making false_factual_claim and source_manipulation strong secondary fits.

value.what_changed_en: Inserted an unsourced qualifier describing the original poems behind the Kalevala as having 'originated in Western Finland and later migrated to Karelia', explicitly intending to claim they were originally Finnish rather than Karelian. Reverted after 29 minutes as an unsourced claim.

value.claim_en: The original poems underlying the Kalevala originated in Western Finland in the Finnish language and only migrated to Karelia later.
value.claim_fi: Kalevalan taustalla olevat alkuperäisrunot ovat syntyneet Länsi-Suomessa suomen kielellä ja siirtyneet Karjalaan vasta myöhemmin.
value.narrative_en: Western Finnish ownership of Kalevala poetry over Karelian heritage
value.historical_note_en: While older nationalist scholarship (such as Julius and Kaarle Krohn's geographic-historical method) argued that Kalevalaic poetry migrated eastward from Western Finland, modern folkloristics recognizes a shared Finnic poetic tradition with deep, independent roots in Karelia and Ingria rather than a purely Western Finnish origin.
value.uncertainty_note: Could also be classified as false_factual_claim or good_faith_error (repeating outdated 19th/early-20th-century schoolbook theories), though the edit summary shows a clear agenda regarding national/linguistic ownership.

value.claim_en: The final poem of the Kalevala prophesies World War II events in 1943, with Väinämöinen representing Russia and Marjatta's son representing a messianic figure baptized by Voitto Viro whose soul was reborn in 1956.
value.claim_fi: Kalevalan viimeinen runo ennustaa vuoden 1943 sotatapahtumia, joissa Väinämöinen kuvaa Venäjää ja Marjatan poika on Voitto Viron kastama messiaaninen hahmo, jonka sielu syntyi uudelleen vuonna 1956.
value.narrative_en: Idiosyncratic eschatological prophecy
value.historical_note_en: The Kalevala was compiled by Elias Lönnrot in the 19th century (1835 and 1849) from traditional Finnic oral folklore and has no connection to World War II or 20th-century individuals.
value.uncertainty_note: The text reads like sincere delusional or fringe religious original research (possibly autobiographical regarding someone born in 1956 and baptized by Voitto Viro), straddling the boundary between false_factual_claim, pov_push, vandalism (due to 'VAGIN', likely a truncation of Vaccinium vitis-idaea or Vacciniaceae rather than intentional obscenity), and other.

value.what_changed_en: Added unsourced claims that the early view of Kalevala poems as purely Karelian gave Svecomans (pro-Swedish nationalists) an opportunity to belittle Finnish-speaking Finns' capacity for folk poetry, changed 'western' origin to 'Finnish, even Western Finnish', and added that according to Mikael Agricola, Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen, and Ahti were Tavastian rather than Karelian gods. Reverted as unsourced ('rv, lähteetöntä').
evidence: Tämä tarjosi [[svekomaanit|svekomaaneille]] oivan tilaisuuden vähätellä suomenkielisten suomalaisten kykyä kansanrunouteen.
Mikael Agricolan mukaan Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen ja Ahti olivat hämäläisten eivätkä karjalaisten jumalia.
value.claim_en: The view that Kalevala poems were solely Karelian enabled Svecomans to disparage Finnish-speakers' poetic abilities, whereas the poems actually had a Finnish or Western Finnish origin, supported by Agricola listing Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen, and Ahti as Tavastian rather than Karelian gods.
value.claim_fi: Näkemys Kalevalan runojen pelkästään karjalaisesta alkuperästä tarjosi svekomaaneille tilaisuuden vähätellä suomenkielisten runokykyä, ja runoilla oli suomalainen tai länsisuomalainen alkuperä, mitä tukee Agricolan maininta Väinämöisestä, Ilmarisesta ja Ahdista hämäläisten jumalina.
value.narrative_en: Fennoman / anti-Svecoman nationalist framing emphasizing the Western Finnish ownership of Kalevala poetry
value.uncertainty_note: Although the claims draw on real 19th-century language-strife debates and Agricola's 1551 list of Tavastian and Karelian gods, the edit injects unsourced nationalist framing ('Finnish, even Western Finnish' contrasted against Karelian, and loaded wording about Svecomans); it sits on the border between pov_push and an unsourced good_faith_error.
